about: Justification trainer prompts for Unit 2 (docs/apcalc-architecture.md, "Justification trainer"). Every number is recomputed in scripts/lib/apcalc-exams.mjs (JUSTIFY_NUMBERS).

prompts.title: A rate from a table, with units
prompts.context:
The temperature of a cup of tea, $T(t)$ degrees Celsius, is measured at selected times $t$ minutes.

$t$ (minutes)0259
$T(t)$ (°C)20263541
prompts.prompt: Estimate $T'(4)$ using the data, and explain what it means. Show the computation and give units.
checklist: Uses the two times closest to $t = 4$ on either side, 2 and 5: $\frac{T(5) - T(2)}{5 - 2}$
Gets $\frac{35 - 26}{3} = 3$ degrees Celsius per minute (units of a rate)
Says what it means: at $t = 4$ minutes the temperature is rising at about 3 degrees Celsius per minute

earns.answer: $T'(4) \approx \frac{T(5) - T(2)}{5 - 2} = \frac{35 - 26}{3} = 3$ degrees Celsius per minute. At time $t = 4$ minutes, the temperature of the tea is increasing at about 3 degrees Celsius per minute.
earns.why: It uses an interval that contains $t = 4$, shows the difference quotient, and gives the answer as a rate with rate units and a time.

misses.why: The interval $[5, 9]$ does not contain $t = 4$, so it estimates the rate at a later time; and "degrees" is the unit of $T$, not of its rate of change.

prompts.title: Differentiable where two pieces meet
prompts.prompt: Is $p$ differentiable at $x = 1$? Justify your answer with limits.
checklist: Shows $p$ is continuous at 1: both one-sided limits equal $1 = p(1)$
Finds the left difference quotient limit: $\lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{(1 + h)^2 - 1}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-} (2 + h) = 2$
Finds the right one: $\lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{2(1 + h) - 1 - 1}{h} = 2$, and concludes $p'(1) = 2$

earns.answer: $\lim_{x \to 1^-} p(x) = 1$, $\lim_{x \to 1^+} p(x) = 2(1) - 1 = 1$ and $p(1) = 1$, so $p$ is continuous at 1. From the left, $\lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{(1 + h)^2 - 1}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-} (2 + h) = 2$. From the right, $\lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{\left(2(1 + h) - 1\right) - 1}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{2h}{h} = 2$. The one-sided limits of the difference quotient agree, so $p$ is differentiable at 1 and $p'(1) = 2$.
earns.why: It shows continuity first and then that both one-sided limits of the difference quotient exist and are equal.

misses.answer: The derivative of $x^2$ is $2x$, which is 2 at $x = 1$, so $p$ is differentiable there.
misses.why: It looks at one piece only. Differentiability at a joining point needs the pieces to meet and the slopes from both sides to agree; with $2x + 1$ as the right piece, this argument would still say yes, wrongly.

prompts.title: Continuous with a corner
prompts.prompt: Explain why $f$ is continuous at $x = 3$ but not differentiable there.
checklist: Finds the one-sided limits of $\frac{f(3 + h) - f(3)}{h} = \frac{|h|}{h}$: $-1$ from the left and 1 from the right
Concludes the derivative does not exist because the one-sided limits differ (a corner)

earns.answer: $\lim_{x \to 3} |x - 3| = 0 = f(3)$, so $f$ is continuous at 3. The difference quotient is $\frac{f(3 + h) - f(3)}{h} = \frac{|h|}{h}$, which is $-1$ for $h < 0$ and 1 for $h > 0$. So $\lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{|h|}{h} = -1$ and $\lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{|h|}{h} = 1$. They are not equal, so $f'(3)$ does not exist: the graph has a corner at $x = 3$.
earns.why: It shows each claim separately, the continuity with a limit and the failure of differentiability with the two one-sided limits of the difference quotient.

misses.answer: $f$ is continuous because there is no hole or jump, and it is not differentiable because the graph has a sharp point.
misses.why: It describes a picture but shows no limits. The scoring guidelines want the reason in terms of the function: the one-sided limits of the difference quotient differ.

prompts.title: What differentiable gives you
prompts.context: The function $g$ is differentiable at $x = 4$, with $g(4) = 7$ and $g'(4) = -2$.
checklist: States that a function differentiable at a point is continuous there
Gives the value 7, and does not use $g'(4)$ for the limit of $g$

earns.answer: Because $g$ is differentiable at $x = 4$, it is continuous at $x = 4$. So $\lim_{x \to 4} g(x) = g(4) = 7$.
earns.why: It names the fact that links the two ideas (differentiable implies continuous) and then uses the definition of continuity.

misses.answer: $\lim_{x \to 4} g(x) = 7$ because you can plug in $x = 4$.
misses.why: Plugging in is allowed only for a function known to be continuous at 4. The answer has to say why $g$ is continuous: it is differentiable there.
